prompt: Which of these are genuine features of QUIC compared with TCP plus TLS? Select all that apply.

options.text: It combines transport and TLS setup and can support eligible 0-RTT early data
options.explanation: Correct. Prior state/configuration is required for early data; rejection, replay concerns, Retry or loss can alter timing.

options.text: Its per-stream ordering avoids making one stream wait solely for missing bytes on another stream
options.explanation: Correct. Shared congestion control, flow control and application dependencies can still affect several streams.

options.text: Connection IDs can support client address changes when migration conditions are satisfied
options.explanation: Correct. Negotiated restrictions, handshake state, usable connection IDs, QUIC path validation and reachability matter; seamless success is not guaranteed.

options.text: It delivers all streams' data in one global order, like TCP
options.explanation: That would reintroduce head-of-line blocking. Ordering is per stream only.

options.text: It is implemented in the OS kernel, which makes it faster to deploy
options.explanation: QUIC can run in user-space libraries or other implementation locations. Its specification does not require a kernel implementation.

workedExample: The first three describe protocol capabilities with their conditions. QUIC does not impose a single global stream delivery order, and its specification does not dictate kernel placement.

prompt: Within a QUIC packet-number space, each newly sent packet gets a new increasing packet number, even when it resends stream data. Which TCP retransmission ambiguity does this remove?

options.text: Packets are smaller, because packet numbers are shorter than sequence numbers
options.explanation: Size isn't the point; QUIC packet numbers can be encoded compactly, but the real gain is unambiguous acknowledgements.

options.text: An ACK identifies which numbered packet transmission arrived, removing original-versus-retransmission ambiguity for that packet
options.explanation: Correct. Other estimation errors and spurious loss declarations remain possible; packet numbers do not make all loss detection infallible.

options.text: Data never needs to be retransmitted
options.explanation: Lost data must still be resent; it is simply sent in a new packet with a new number, with stream offsets keeping the data's position.

options.text: It allows middleboxes to reorder packets correctly
options.explanation: Packet numbers have header protection. An observer can derive Initial protection keys, so “middleboxes can never read any packet numbers” would also be too strong.

workedExample: TCP reuses byte sequence numbers when resending data, so an ACK may not reveal which copy caused it; Karn’s rule or timestamps address RTT-sampling ambiguity. QUIC identifies packet transmissions separately from stream offsets, within each packet-number space. This removes that particular ambiguity. ACK delay, sampling choices and reordering still require careful recovery logic.

link.title: RFC 9002: QUIC Loss Detection and Congestion Control

prompt: A phone loses its old Wi-Fi path and gains a new address on 5G. Compare ordinary TCP (without MPTCP or an address-preserving tunnel) with a confirmed QUIC connection using usable connection IDs. Assume active migration is allowed and the new path passes validation and remains reachable. Which connection can continue at the transport level?

options.text: Both continue seamlessly, because the server recognises the device
options.explanation: TCP has no concept of a device; a connection is its 4-tuple. A new client IP is a different connection as far as TCP is concerned.

options.text: Both break; the application must resume the download in either case
options.explanation: Under the supplied conditions, QUIC can migrate the existing connection to the new path.

options.text: Ordinary TCP cannot move the existing connection to the new address; QUIC can continue through migration
options.explanation: Correct under the stated assumptions. QUIC still needs appropriate QUIC path validation and congestion-control handling; this does not promise no interruption.

options.text: The QUIC connection breaks but TCP continues, because TCP retransmits to the new address
options.explanation: TCP has no way to change a connection's addresses. Segments from the new IP don't match any existing connection.

workedExample: Ordinary TCP identifies the connection by its endpoint addresses and ports, so the stated address change cannot simply retarget it. An application can reconnect and resume if its protocol supports that. QUIC connection IDs allow the established connection to be found from a new address; validation and path-state changes still apply. The question explicitly supplies successful migration conditions rather than assuming every network change succeeds.
